headline: Toronto Met Discovers Diversity Statements Don't Cure Antisemitism
subheadline: The Benotto report reveals that corporate values documents are excellent at making boards feel virtuous while faculty hide their faith.
source_headline: Howard Levitt: Toronto Metropolitan University has a problem that no diversity statement can solve
body_html:
Toronto Metropolitan University has discovered something institutional leaders have spent decades trying to paper over with mission statements and equity task forces: you cannot resolve systemic discrimination by publishing a well-crafted commitment to inclusion. The Benotto report, commissioned to investigate workplace culture, found that some faculty and staff at the institution actively concealed their Jewish identity out of fear—a detail so stark it makes every laminated diversity poster in the administrative wing look like performance art. This is not a disagreement about curriculum or a misunderstanding about pronouns. This is people choosing invisibility over safety, which suggests that whatever Toronto Met's official values document promises, the actual lived experience on campus tells a different story entirely.

The problem Howard Levitt identifies in his analysis cuts to the heart of institutional hypocrisy: a university—an organization ostensibly devoted to intellectual freedom and inclusive community—has somehow created an environment where people must hide a fundamental part of their identity. The Benotto findings reveal that this isn't theoretical or anecdotal; it's documented behavior among staff and faculty who reasonably assessed that being openly Jewish carried professional or social risk. No amount of rebranding, no new Chief Diversity Officer hire, no mandatory training session can retrofit an institution once trust has fractured at that level. The gap between what Toronto Met claims to stand for and what employees actually experience is not a communication problem that better PR can solve—it's a values problem.

What makes this particularly mordant is the timing and the irony: institutions across North America have spent the last decade issuing increasingly elaborate diversity statements, each one more comprehensive and earnest than the last. They've appointed committees, launched initiatives, and hired consultants. They've created the infrastructure of inclusion while apparently doing nothing about the conditions that make people afraid to exist authentically in their own workplaces. Toronto Met's situation suggests that all those statements functioned less as guardrails and more as cover—visible commitments that satisfied external stakeholders while internal culture remained hostile enough to drive people underground. The Benotto report is essentially documentation of what that gap looks like when you stop ignoring it.

Consider what institutional leadership was presumably hoping for when those diversity statements were drafted: plausible deniability, a shield against criticism, visible commitment without operational upheaval. The theory, such as it is, goes like this: publish a strong values statement, and culture will follow. Reality, apparently, does not work that way. You cannot mandate belonging through a press release. The fact that university employees felt compelled to hide their religion suggests something far more serious than a content problem—it suggests a culture problem, one that predates and outlasts any official policy. A diversity statement functions as a kind of institutional permission slip, a way for leadership to claim they've addressed an issue without actually addressing it.

The broader scandal here is not that Toronto Met has an antisemitism problem—many institutions do, and many refuse to acknowledge it—but that the institution assembled what appears to be a comprehensive values framework and still managed to create conditions where people hid their identity. That's not a failure of language. That's a failure of institutional will. The Benotto report exists because someone finally asked the obvious question: does anyone actually believe what the website says? The answer, it turns out, is no. And no amount of revised copy will change that until the people running the institution demonstrate that they mean it through structural change, not just linguistic commitment.

What's particularly rich is watching the gap between aspirational institutional communication and actual employee experience widen in real time. Universities, more than almost any other sector, trade in the currency of values and enlightenment. They claim to be spaces where difficult truths are examined and diverse perspectives are protected. Toronto Met's discovery that some of its own community members felt unsafe enough to hide their religion is the kind of data point that should trigger existential institutional soul-searching, not a PR response. The Benotto report is essentially evidence that institutional diversity statements function primarily as theater—necessary for accreditation and donor relations, useless for actually changing how people behave when no one official is watching.

The real lesson here, for Toronto Met and every other institution reflexively drafting stronger values language, is this: culture does not follow policy. Culture precedes policy and determines whether policy means anything at all. You can promise equity and inclusion and respect until your communications department runs out of synonyms, but if people are hiding who they are to feel safe, your values document is just expensive wallpaper.
glossary_definition: A publicly displayed institutional commitment to inclusion that creates the appearance of addressing discrimination while allowing the actual conditions that drive discrimination to persist unmolested.
